messages.subject_clean: questions on: # of dispersal events inferred from one area to another; states_list argument
messages.body_plain:
Dear BioGeoBEARS users, I have few questions, maybe someone can help me with those:

1 - Is it possible to get the “number of events” inferred by the model? For example, number of dispersal events from one area to another, number of range expansion and range contraction events. If this is possible, how could I get that?

2 - I'd like to use the function infprobs_to_probs_of_each_area_from_relprobs to have the probability of presence in each area. However, how do I get the “states_list” argument? (required by the function). As far as I understood, this list refers to the possible states/geographic ranges coded as variables in the marginal probabilities matrix (result$ML_marginal_prob_each_state_at_branch_top_AT_node). Is this right?

3 - Last: Is it possible to remove the ranges from the tips when plotting the reconstruction? They sometimes overlap and hide the species names, so I'd like to keep just the range of internal nodes. I tried to omit the argument tipranges but the function didn't work.

Thank you!

Silvia

messages.body_plain:
Hi Manuel,

Sorry it took a bit for me to get back to this.  I don't think I programmed a ready way to do a pie-chart of all of the states from a Lagrange output.  IIRC Lagrange just gives probabilities of the states/ranges that occupy the top 95% of the probability, not the probabilities of all of the states, so (1) they don't add up to 100% and (2) the states list will be different for each node, making the programming and coloring more complex.  It would be solvable, but -- it would be way easier to just run DEC in BioGeoBEARS and use those pie charts!

If you really wanted to do it anyway, you could take the table provided by e.g. LGpy_splits_fn_to_table, convert this to a table with the nodes in rows and the state probabilities in columns, and then plot pie charts on the tree yourself using the "pie" option in ape's plot.phylo -- this is basically what BioGeoBEARS is doing anyway.

Cheers!
Nick

messages.body_plain:
I already emailed Silvia some of these answers, but briefly:

On Wednesday, October 1, 2014 12:29:20 PM UTC-4, Silvia Pavan wrote:
>
> Dear BioGeoBEARS users, I have few questions, maybe someone can help me with those:
>
> 1 - Is it possible to get the “number of events” inferred by the model? For example, number of dispersal events from one area to another, number of range expansion and range contraction events. If this is possible, how could I get that?

The best way to count events is with stochastic mapping, see:

The plot of most-probable states is not the same thing as an estimate of event counts
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#Most_prob_states_not_events

The right way to count events -- Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping (BSM)
http://phylo.wikidot.com/per-event-weights-of-cladogenetic-range-inheritance-events-i#BSM

(Note that these event counts are counts given the model, data, and the assumption the observed tree is the complete tree -- obviously the latter is usually false, so what you are really counting is "events that have evidence preserved on the observed tree".)

> 2 - I'd like to use the function infprobs_to_probs_of_each_area_from_relprobs to have the probability of presence in each area. However, how do I get the “states_list” argument? (required by the function). As far as I understood, this list refers to the possible states/geographic ranges coded as variables in the marginal probabilities matrix (result$ML_marginal_prob_each_state_at_branch_top_AT_node). Is this right?

You can get states_list with cladoRcpp's rcpp_areas_list_to_states_list:

(this function uses C++ to make it fast, so it's in cladoRcpp rather than BioGeoBEARS)

============

library(cladoRcpp)

# Specify the areas
areas_list = c("A", "B", "C")
areas_list

# Calculate the list of 0-based indices for each possible geographic range, i.e.
# each combination of areas

states_list = rcpp_areas_list_to_states_list(areas=areas_list, maxareas=3,
include_null_range=FALSE)
states_list

states_list = rcpp_areas_list_to_states_list(areas=areas_list, maxareas=2,
include_null_range=TRUE)
states_list

============

...you can then modify the states_list by hand if you want to remove certain "impossible" ranges.

>
> 3 - Last: Is it possible to remove the ranges from the tips when plotting the reconstruction? They sometimes overlap and hide the species names, so I'd like to keep just the range of internal nodes. I tried to omit the argument tipranges but the function didn't work.

I think if you set show.tip.label=FALSE, this should remove the species names, at least if you are using the most up-to-date version of BioGeoBEARS_plots_v1.R, sourced here:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#script

Alternatively, you can moving the species names further to the right with label.offset, or shrinking the labels or the states with tipcex, statecex, splitcex, etc. These work basically similarly to options in ape's plot.phylo.

(PS in R-land, cex= "character expansion")

 Cheers!
Nick

> Thank you!
>
> Silvia

messages.subject: Re: error in BiogeoBEARS
messages.body_plain:
Hi Julian,

You are getting this error, just translated:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/biogeobears/nan$20function$20call/biogeobears/U1rFQPYy6G8/82VWzEMelCMJ

Error in rexpokit::expokit_dgpadm_Qmat(Qmat = Qmat, t = times, transpose_needed) :
  NA/NaN/Inf in foreign function call (arg 4)

Also, when you get the NaN crash, then you will not get stored results for that model, so the AIC calculations etc. at the end will not work.

So, you should adjust the min/max for DIVALIKE+J etc.  Also, run the models one-at-a-time, if you just copy-paste all six models at once, you won't see which models worked and which didn't. Once you get one model working, go on to the next.  You can set runslow=FALSE for a model after it has worked once, then you don't have to keep re-running it.

Cheers!
Nick

messages.subject: likelihood of constrained vs unconstrained
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

We are analyzing a large dataset of ~1000 sp. with 5 area states.  We get higher likelihoods when we enforce our own matrix of dispersal multipliers than when the analysis is unconstrained.  On one hand this seems good (like our matrix reflect real differences in dispersal probability between different areas in different time slices), but it is also counterintuitive because likelihoods should always be worse with constrained models.  For example, with nucleotide models, K2P will always have a higher likelihood than JC because the transition rate is not constrained to equal the transversion rate.  But perhaps we are thinking about this incorrectly -- that the imposed dispersal multiplier matrix is not exactly a constraint?  I do see that the two models have the same number of parameters, so the comparison with JC and K2P is not quite analogous.  Also curious to know if others have had this result.

Thanks,

Stacey
messages.body_snippet:
Hi all,

We are analyzing a large dataset of ~1000 sp. with 5 area states.  We get higher likelihoods when we enforce our own matrix of dispersal multipliers than when the analysis is unconstrained.

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] likelihood of constrained vs unconstrained
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stacey!  I would think about it this way:

1. If you take a model (model A) with n free parameters, and add another free parameter (making model B), model B will always have the same or higher likelihood.  This is because model B contains model A, so its ML solution can never have lower likelihood than model A's ML solution.

(If you do get model B lower than model A, this means your maximum likelihood (ML) search failed to optimize completely for some reason, which can happen, since the standard search algorithms are heuristic and not necessarily perfect.)

( 1a. If you add a free parameter that is useless, you will still improve the likelihood a little bit. However, this will probably not be statistically significant -- more specifically, it will be statistically significant at the p<0.05 cutoff only 5% of the time. )

2. There is no such hard rule for two models if the models are non-nested. As a rule of thumb, models with more free parameters will probably be able to fit the data better, but really this all depends on the structure of the models and data.

3. There is also no such rule if two models differ in various fixed parameters.  These could help or hurt the likelihood, depending.  E.g.:

- If one had a dataset with 100 subclades with topology (A,(A,(A,B)), and only one subclade with (A,(A,(A,C))),

- then if one had a fixed model specifying that the probability of dispersal between A and B was fixed to be 100 times higher than the probability of dispersal between A and C

- then that fixed model would confer higher likelihood on the data than an "unconstrained" fixed dispersal model, which assumes equal rates between all areas.

Probably what is confusing is that the word "constrained" means somewhat different things in different contexts, e.g.:

- constraining free parameters to take a fixed value

- constraining dispersal modifiers from "unconstrained" (fixed equal rates between regions) to fixed unequal rates between regions

Cheers!
Nick

On Mon, Oct 13, 2014 at 6:41 PM, Stacey Smith <dewi...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi all,
>
> We are analyzing a large dataset of ~1000 sp. with 5 area states.  We get higher likelihoods when we enforce our own matrix of dispersal multipliers than when the analysis is unconstrained.  On one hand this seems good (like our matrix reflect real differences in dispersal probability between different areas in different time slices), but it is also counterintuitive because likelihoods should always be worse with constrained models.  For example, with nucleotide models, K2P will always have a higher likelihood than JC because the transition rate is not constrained to equal the transversion rate.  But perhaps we are thinking about this incorrectly -- that the imposed dispersal multiplier matrix is not exactly a constraint?  I do see that the two models have the same number of parameters, so the comparison with JC and K2P is not quite analogous.  Also curious to know if others have had this result.
>
> Thanks,
>
> Stacey
